Figure 1:Narrow-boundary safety.A deployment-specific policy may need to refuse only political prompts that ask
for manipulation, propaganda, or targeted persuasion (the target-harmful subset,
later formalised asHH), while still answering other political prompts (the
benign complement,Ω∖H\Omega\setminus H), rather than refusing all of politics
(Ω\Omega). A trained model’s refusal behaviour, a probability in[0,1][0,1], is smoother
than this ideal split and can overshoot into benign territory near the boundary. The marked
fake-harmful region shows the downside of raising refusal for surface-dangerous
benign prompts, tested directly infig.5.

Figure 2:Coverage gap in self-generated safety data.Steering a harmful prompt does not always produce a refusal. Prompts where
steering succeeds form the refusal preimagef−1​(Ref)f^{-1}(\mathrm{Ref}); prompts
where it fails form the drop setD=H∖f−1​(Ref)D=H\setminus f^{-1}(\mathrm{Ref}).Section4introduces constructions that recover these failed
